# When do bugs see (infra)red? On the Visual and Infra-red in the Insect Perceptual Apparatus

the bull case for applying a vibrational theory of olfaction to insect chemosensing  
   
Tucker Chambers, Daniel A. Friedman

# Abstract {#abstract}

Olfaction, Vision, and other sensory modalities interact to shape behavior and learning across the natural world, for example in insects. In this paper, we:

* **Review several disparate bodies of empirical entomological evidence**, with an open eye and mind to the effects of visual and non-visual photonic spectra.   
* Pay specific attention to the interesting **convergence of evidence from multiple domains upon the infra-red wavelength range**.   
* Primarily we consider the **phenomena of vision & chemosensation (olfaction)** and where a broader understanding of the biological relevance of infra-red light may lead to unique explanations, predictions, and experiments.   
  * We suggest that i**ncluding the possible mechanism of infra-red influence on olfaction could augment traditional semiochemical receptor-based accounts**, drawing on models of insect antennal sensilla as dielectric waveguides and a resonating mixed-phase meta-material.   
* **Within Entomology**, in the perceptual domains of vision, olfaction, and possible bioelectric signaling, we speculate on the role of infra-red light in many cognitive and behavioral phenomena, such as nestmate recognition in eusocial Hymenoptera, sexual and trail pheromone detection, necrophoresis, parasite-host interactions, and more.  
* **Beyond Entomology**, we briefly sketch some implications of a fuller understanding of infra-red light’s entomological function, across domains such as: cognitive-behavioral, agronomical, evolutionary-ecological, and collective intelligence. 


# Introduction {#introduction}

Olfaction is the ability to detect free-floating molecules in an organism’s immediate environment, a sense known as “smell”. It is a well-conserved trait across biology, with broad functional and neurological similarities across diverse taxa \[42\]. In more specific terms, olfaction is the observed relationship between a volatile stimulus’ presence, its proximal arrival to a sensory organ (such as a nose or antenna), and the corresponding neurological response and organismal behavior. This paper will be focusing in particular on olfaction in Insecta.

See \[32\] for a concise summary of the several predominant theories of olfaction. In general, the classical theories of olfaction are based on the shape of molecules and their corresponding fit with differentially selective olfactory receptors (ORs) found on the cellular membranes of olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs). This is known as the stereochemical theory of olfaction, or the lock-and-key method — an odor molecule “fits” or “docks” with a specific receptor, and initiates an ionic cascade that becomes a measurable neural response. It is has been found that individual odors can fit with many different ORs during one sensing event, and so even with a relatively restricted set of ORs (there are only hundreds of known receptor types, but billions of perceptible odors), it is theorized that their combinatorial activation allows for high-precision odor encoding despite most receptors having general low specificity (i.e. broadly tuned). 

![][image1]  
Original caption from \[46\]: COMBINATORIAL CODING INCLUDING BROADLY TUNED ODORANT RECEPTORS (OR) CONTRASTED WITH SPECIALIZED ORS ACTIVATING DEDICATED NEURONAL PATHWAYS. (A) With combinatorial coding (left), each odorant binds to several receptors with overlapping ligand affinities, and each OR is activated by multiple ligands. In contrast, specific ORs for ecologically relevant cues are activated by one or a few structurally related odorants, and little cross-activation of ORs occurs (right). (B) With combinatorial coding, a single odorant activates a unique combination of glomeruli in the antennal lobe (left) due to binding to multiple ORs, whereas a single odorant activates a single glomerulus in a system comprised of specialized ORs and dedicated channels (right).

The stereochemical theory of olfaction has several limitations. The most salient is the fact that molecules that have near-identical shapes and chemical structures, and would thus have similar effects on ORs, have been found instead to have different odors and incite different behavioral and neurological responses. \[44, 45\] 

	![][image2]  
Image from \[44\]: models of ferrocene (left) and nickelocene (right), which have different odors yet identical shapes. In terms of vibrational mode, however, they have measurably different signatures. Examples such as this refute a stereochemical theory of olfaction. 

This evidence has been elaborated on with studies investigating ORN responses to deuterated homologues of known odor molecules. Deuteration is the substitution of natural hydrogen with a heavier isotope. This affects the weight (and emission spectra) of a molecule, but not its shape. Studies on mammalian and insect ORNs, both with extracted neurons and via behavioral conditioning assays, demonstrate that deuteration does in fact elicit unique responses and that deuterated homologues “smell” differently. This strongly suggests that olfaction is not primarily mediated at receptor surfaces. \[30, 43, 44\]

Another limitation of the stereochemical theory of olfaction is its possible incompatibility with super low-latency ORN reaction times, reported on the order of 1 to 5 ms in insects. \[15, 25, 26\] observe (or attribute) low latency detection by putatively “olfactive” (i.e. stereoscopic) ORs to fast transport of volatile molecules from the antennal surface into antennal pores. They reported neuronal responses to olfactory stimuli occurring an order of magnitude faster than what has otherwise been found to be the lower bound of olfactory response times. However, these papers rely on questionable assumptions. For example, in \[27\], which is cited as corroboratory evidence for uncharacteristically fast olfaction in \[15\], they base their "time from contact to dendrite" of 1ms on a diffusion equation that makes two important assumptions, which may very well make their assumed time of 1ms significantly inaccurate. The first, is that the viscosity of sensilla lymph, which affects diffusion speeds across sensilla surfaces, is assumed to be 0.002 Pascal-seconds. However, other quantitative and qualitative values measured for sensilla lymph are much more viscous, by 50x or more \[49\]. The second assumption they made is that the distance that the diffusing semiochemical must travel is 300 nm, because that is a typical depth of a sensilla pore. This ignores the lateral distance the semiochemical must travel along the exterior surface of the sensilla, between whose pores there can be distances of several hundred nanometers as well. Both of these assumptions and their possible inaccuracy undermine the credibility of their subsequent assumption of a very fast 1ms timing of antennal contact to signal transduction. 

Is it possible that these observed low latency responses are due to an alternative mechanism, and not to a stereochemical olfactory response that is an order of magnitude faster than what had been previously understood as the lower bound of insect and mammalian olfaction?  
From \[15\]:  "The minimum first spike latency \[neuron-to-neuron\] jitter of 0.19 ms is more than one order of magnitude smaller than previously reported for insect olfactory receptor neurons (7 ms jitter \[Jeanne and Wilson, 2015\]) or for vertebrate olfactory receptor neurons (12 ms jitter \[Shusterman et al., 2011\]). Such a high spike timing precision is comparable with the precision of insect photoreceptor cells (0.1 ms jitter \[Tatler et al., 2000\]) or insect auditory receptor cells (0.16 ms jitter \[Rokem et al., 2005\]).” Interestingly, the low latency comparison in insects — photo and auditory receptors — both deal with wave detection, not chemical detection. Would it seem plausible, then, that the low latency of the "olfactive" response might also be due in fact to wave detection, i.e. (infrared) radiant waves being emitted by the semiochemicals and picked up by the antennal sensilla? 

Finally, stereoscopic theories of insect olfaction do not typically account for the ultrastructural morphology and spatial arrangement of the sensory organs believed to be the epicenters of olfaction across all insects; namely, the micron-sized hair-like sensilla that line insect antennae and which will be the focus of a subsequent section.

Admittedly, much remains unknown about ligand-receptor interactions at the molecular level, but evidence is growing that molecular shape alone is not sufficient for explaining olfaction, and that different (or perhaps multi-modal) sensing regimes are essential for the detection and discrimination of odorants. 

## The vibrational theory of olfaction {#the-vibrational-theory-of-olfaction}

The vibrational, or spectroscopic, theory of olfaction proposes that it is the unique electromagnetic radiation emitted by free-floating odor molecules that animals are detecting, rather than geometric or chemical information at the binding surface of ORs. 

A compelling circumstance in support of the vibrational theory is the fact that the Earth’s atmosphere has transmission windows in the mid- and long-infrared (2 to 30+ microns), precisely in the range of electromagnetic emissions from semiochemicals like cuticular hydrocarbons and pheromones. This means that radiation at these wavelengths can travel more or less freely, and therefore be leveraged by organisms for sensing and communication.   
![][image3]  
Atmospheric windows

Just as many terrestrial lifeforms have developed sensing capabilities and behaviors dependent on the visible and ultraviolet spectra of light, it is natural that they would likewise develop sensing and behavior responsive to the informationally-available infrared spectra.

Induced mutation experiments investigating the selective sensitivities of insect ORs, which knock out the expression of specific genes, have shown that knocking out ORs associated with odors that share similar emission spectra will affect perception for all odors emitting in the corresponding frequency range. This is analogous to photoreception experiments that knock out the expression of long-wavelength cones and thereby induce protanopia. \[44\]

An important perceptual advantage made possible by vibrationally-sensitive sensilla, and not possible with a lock-and-key model of olfaction, is the ability to extract additional information encoded in the vibratory behavior of odor molecules. Free-floating odor molecules interact with their environment in concentration-dependent ways. The presence of water vapor, for example, can cause phase shifts in the emitted radiation of a pheromone as a function of their respective concentrations through a process known as Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET). In FRET, energy from excited water molecules can be transferred to pheromone molecules, creating detectable phase shifts and/or other changes in the emission spectra of the pheromones. This phenomenon may be used by sensilla to not only detect a semiochemical’s presence, concentration, and direction, but also decode pertinent information about it’s proximity. The image below from \[6\] provides a concise example in the cabbage looper moth. 

![][image4]

The vibrational theory is not without its limitations and critics \[48, 50\]. A frequent criticism is that enantiomers, or chiral variants of a chemical compound, would be indifferentiable in a spectroscopic system because it is presumed that, being only distinguishable as “handedness” or mirror-image variations of the same compound, they would have identical emission frequencies and therefore be olfactively indistinguishable. Some experiments though have found them to have different odors, undermining a vibrational interpretation. However, advances in experimental spectroscopy have shown detectable variations in emission spectra of enantiomers. \[34\] Further experimentation is needed, but it is now clear that in principle enantiomer distinction is not incompatible with a vibrational theory of olfaction.

\[55\] offers a fairly complete rebuke of \[6\].

## Olfaction in Insecta {#olfaction-in-insecta}

The set of genetically-encoded insect ORs is one of the largest and most diverse found in biology, which speaks to this olfaction’s primacy in the ethology, survival, and evolution of Insecta. \[47\] As opposed to vertebrate ORs, which are mostly metabotropic, in which signal cascades are mediated secondary chemicals, insect ORs are ionotropic, or direct ligand-gated cation channels. \[23, 45\] This design allows for rapid signal transduction, which is typically found to be faster in insects \[15, 23\]. 

![][image5]  
Image and caption from \[23\]: Signaling mechanisms of mammalian and insect odorant receptors. A schematic of the molecular basis of olfactory signal transduction in the mouse and fruit fly. ACIII, type III adenylyl cyclase; ATP, adenosine triphosphate; cAMP, cyclic adenosine monophosphate; ANO2, anoctamin 2 channel; CNG, cyclic nucleotide-gated channel;.Gαolf, olfactory G protein α-subunit; OR, odorant receptor.

Insects inhabit a moleculary-rich world, full of exogenous and endogenous chemicals that they use for a wide range of behaviors, from conspecific recognition to predation, reproduction to necrophoresis. Being able to detect and react to semiochemical stimuli with low latency and high precision confers obvious advantages. Here we will lay out the evidence for insect olfaction being dependent on detecting molecular vibrations of semiochemicals in the infrared range via the micron-sized hair-like sensilla that cover their antennae. 

## Morphological evidence {#morphological-evidence}

All adult insects have antennae, and all insect antennae have micron-sized sensory hairs called sensilla. Even larvae are covered in structurally similar sensilla \[29\]. There are dozen or so categorized sensilla types, largely conserved across Insecta, of which the sensilla trichodea, sensilla basiconica, and sensilla coeloconica are believed to be central to olfaction because of their porous surface[^1]. It’s possible that all forms forms of antenna-borne sensilla are involved in olfaction in some way, but the objective of this paper is not to be an exhaustive review or analysis of sensilla types and function, but rather to make the case that morphological, neurological, behavioral, and experimental evidence of sensilla demonstrates their spectroscopic capabilities and thereby illustrates the inherently vibratory nature of olfaction specifically and insect ethology more broadly.  
![][image6]![][image7]  
Image source: \[6\]

Thinking back to the available atmospheric transmission windows in the infrared range, insects seem particularly well-adapted to exploit these informational niches. Insect semiochemicals, such as cuticular hydrocarbons (CHCs) and pheromones, have emission spectra squarely within transmission windows. And, not surprisingly, the hair-like sensilla on insect antennae have micrometric dimensions that correspond closely to the wavelengths of insect semiochemicals. For example, hydrocarbon trail pheromones in fire ants have an emission peak around 3500 cm^-1 (\~2.9 microns) \[24\]; and the cabbage looper moth sex pheromone emits peaks at 17 and 26 microns.[^2]  
![][image8]  
Image from \[24\]

Sensilla are covered in CHCs, like the rest of the insect exoskeleton. CHCs are essential for a wide range of insect adaptations and behaviors, such as nestmate recognition (more on that later) and water retention. While they themselves are important semiochemicals, they appear to also play an essential role in the mechanisms olfaction. CHCs are typically non-polar molecules but can become dielectric in the presence of electric fields, like the kinds induced by the dendritic neurons and negatively-charged sensilla lumen that populate the interior of insect sensilla \[35\]. This induced dialecticism of CHC coatings has been found to play an important role in the attraction of free-floating semiochemicals to sensilla surfaces. \[6, 16\] Once an odor molecule arrives in proximity or contact with a sensilla, how is it detected and decoded according to the vibrational theory?  
![][image9]  
From wikimedia commons, the general ultrastructure of a   
porous sensillum (in this case, a basiconic type)  [link](https://en.m.wikibooks.org/wiki/File:Schematic_insect_basiconic_sensillum.png)

In the 1960’s and 1970’s, Dr. Philip S. Callahan and others laid out the theoretical and experimental groundwork for understanding insect antennae as dielectric waveguides and electromagnetic resonators capable of, and particularly evolved for, detecting and amplifying infrared radiation from species-specific semiochemicals. \[6\]

In general, traditional theories of olfaction based on antenna sensilla don’t account for the geometric arrangement and morphology of olfactory sensilla \[5\], which when taken into full account seem well-evolved for waveguiding and infrared detection. These interpretations and much of the related experimentation in olfaction focus their work starting from the point of contact between odor molecules and OR surfaces, or sometimes including in-pore phenomena as well such as protein-facilitated transport of odor molecules to ORs. But a full theory of olfaction ought to take into account the sensilla ultrastructures that are central to it across all insect taxa and integrate their morphology, function, and electric and chemical properties. A strong argument in favor of the vibrational theory of olfaction is that it does just this. 

Indeed in \[6\], as seen in the images below, all insect antenna sensilla are matched with human-engineered antenna equivalents, explaining them in terms of their 1\) physical dimensions, 2\) dielectric properties 3), heterogeneous CHC coatings, 4\) pores, 5\) their surface sculpturing, 6\) their form, 7\) their natural and induced vibratory frequencies, 8\) the arrangements (arrays) of groups of sensilla, and 9\) antenna-related behaviors like grooming, rubbing, and sweeping. Such a full accounting of the morphology, properties, and function of sensilla as electromagnetic antennae lends credibility and evidence to the idea that insect antennae are in fact complex, species-specific electromagnetic detectors (though not exclusively, of course). 

![][image10] ![][image11]![][image12]

Images from \[6\]. Each image shows a diagram of a standard engineered antenna type, paired with its corresponding sensilla type, based on its morphology and proposed absorption behavior.

The pores that line most kinds of insect sensilla are putatively understood to be conduits that guide odor molecules to ORN dendrites in sensillum interior. However, \[6\] offers an alternative, or at least complementary function of sensilla pores, that facilitates their spectroscopic sensitivity. “It has been demonstrated both theoretically and experimentally that in order to increase the gain (an increase in power of a transmitted signal) that the tube wall of a dielectric antenna be designed with walls as thin as possible. The ultimate technique would be to produce a wall so thin that it has no structural integrity at all. This, of course, is not possible, either in nature or in man-made structures. Fortunately, a more practical technique is available for electrically accomplishing the same end and thus effectively reducing the dielectric constant of the tube wall--that is, by perforating the wall with multitudes of small holes. The auricillicum sensilla is an excellent example of this technique applied in nature.” In other words, if sensilla are in fact dielectric terahertz frequency antennas, then their pores serve a functionally critical role separate from their possible role, ancillary or otherwise, of conducting odor molecules towards OR surfaces inside the sensilla. 

![][image13]  
From \[6\], showing auricillicum sensillum and its pores.

It is fascinating to look at cross sections of innervated sensilla (below, left) and compare them to similar diagrams of multi-rod antennas (below, right). The parallel dendritic branches of ORNs correspond to the parallel receptors of multi-rod antennas. Multi-rod antenna arrays contribute to signal gain, effectively amplifying a detected frequency thereby facilitating its detection and propagation.  

![][image14] ![][image15]  
Images from  \[16, Fig. 12\] and \[6, Fig. 1\]

Cross-sections of individual ORN dendrites reveal that they are dense in parallel microtubules (MTs). See the image below. From \[35\]: “A conspicuous density of microtubules is observed in the voluminous dendritic outer segment of thermo- and hygroreceptors. The question of whether these tubules are to be regarded as cytoskeleton elements that support the fine dendritic processes or whether they take part in transduction remains unresolved.” The particular role of MTs in these dendrites is indeed unknown, but it is interesting to consider that MTs are piezoelectric \[37\], can absorb and transmit electromagnetic energy, and are arranged in parallel arrays that would facilitate. Microtubules are piezoelectric and responsive to frequencies in the micron range. \[39\] It has been found that the parallel microtubules in a sensilla can be disassembled with colchicine and vinblastine, and that this renders the sensilla non-responsive. \[36\] Consider the density and array of MTs as seen in this sensilla cross-section:

## Neurological evidence {#neurological-evidence}

Another aspect of insect olfaction is the notably rapid response rates measured between odor molecule arrival to antennae-bound sensilla and neural spikes. As mentioned previously, a vibrational system of primary olfaction, which would not require odor absorption, diffusion into pores, and contact with ORs, could account for the very low-latency response times of insect olfaction. As stated in \[23\]: “Analyses of insect OSN responses to artificial odour plumes have demonstrated their ability to rapidly track the presence or absence of odours through changes in action potential frequency... Such fast behavioural responses require both the onset and the termination of cellular responses to the stimuli to be fast. In these cases, an ionotropic mechanism might also be advantageous, because the dissociation of an odour molecule from the receptor could lead to rapid channel closure.” Could it be that vibratory detection is multi-modal with broadly-tuned ligand-receptor detection, to permit high-precision, low-latency odor resolution via the quasi-immediate detection of proximate molecular radiation, while the absorption and (redundant) detection by the in-pore ORs regulate secondary phenomena like signal adaptation or termination, and that together they form a more robust and olfactory system?

To further support a multimodal model, there is some evidence that insects can integrate visual and infrared sensory information, from compound eyes and infrared organs respectively, to guide foraging and reproductive behaviors. \[51\] A theory put forth by \[45\] of the role of quantum electron tunneling in ligand-receptor interactions, mediated by resonant modes, may provide a possible connecting phenomenon between vibrational and stereoscopic olfaction mechanisms. 

## Behavioral evidence {#behavioral-evidence}

If the sensilla hairs are indeed acting like directional antenna, this would explain observed self-orienting of the hairs in the direction of odors, which can be thought of as a means of focusing the narrow beam directional antennal hairs towards the source of radiant emission, increasing their effectiveness. 

\[52\] describes known infrared sensors in two beetle species, supposed to have evolved from hair-like mechanoreceptors. The existence and evolution of these hair-like sensors lays a foundation for analyzing the possible development and evolution of infrared sensitivity in antennal hair-like receptors.

	\[23\] found differential expression of ORs in worker ants as a function of task (e.g. nurses vs. foragers). An interesting experiment would be to look at how ORs changes in individuals over their lifetime, as a function of their task. In social hymenoptera workers have age-dependent tasks, and thus possibly different OR expressions at different points in their life. Could OR expression be induced by e.g. strong stimulus association with food in lab?   
	There is an analogy here with the immune system, with differential expression based on environment and conditioned experience. Can the olfactory system also learn and self-tune over the course of a lifetime? Can this be passed on, in a Lamarckian fashion, to immediate generations?

# Trimmings

# However, for an idea as ubiquitous and intuitive as “smell”, olfaction is surprisingly not very well understood, with much of its biophysical and neural underpinnings remaining poorly understood. Classical theories of olfaction, like the ligand-receptor “lock-and-key” model, are being challenged by alternative theories that purport to better explain its high-sensitivity and low-latency nature and correspond more closely to its associated morphologies and behaviors. In light of a growing body of morphological, neurological, behavioral, and experimental evidence, the theory that olfaction is in fact a form of electromagnetic sensitivity, that it is a vibrational sense anchored in spectroscopic detection of infrared molecular emissions, is increasingly promising.

“To illuminate the midges during this time, we use several arrays of infrared light-emitting diodes (LEDs), placed inside and on top of the enclosure; i**nfrared light is invisible to the midges** but can be captured by our cameras.” This is said again and again across research.

Ultrastructure analyses of sensilla types typically take for granted that aporous sensilla must not be involved in olfaction; for example see \[52\] 

[^2]:  See \[6, p. 387-388\] for a more in-depth exposition of the physics of antenna dimensions and ideal wavelength detection: “Since the length of the dielectric rod or tube has a greater effect on beam width than-does the diameter, then as L/A o increases, the width of the main beam decreases. Extremely efficient narrow band antennas (sharp frequency tuning) can be designed between 2 and 6 wavelengths in length if the taper is sufficient to reduce the unwanted side lobes of radiation. It is evident then that if an antenna is designed to have no interfering side lobes it should be designed shorter than 2-wavelengths long. If an extremely narrow band (sharp frequency tuning) directional antenna is desired it should be between 2- and 6-wavelengths long and tapered in such a way as to reduce side lobe interference. Based on design criteria, we should expect that in regard to length most sensilla will resonate to wavelengths from ca. 1 to 1/6 sensillum lengths. The simplest form of such a dielectric antenna system is the straight, tapered sensilla trichodea. Later we shall examine this basic type antenna, but for purposes of design criteria it is sufficient to point out here that most trichodea range from 6 to 160µm in length. A sensilla trichodea 6µm long at 1 λ would resonate in the 6µm region. A trichodea 160µm in length and 6 λ long would resonate in the 26.67µm region. If on the other hand the 160µm sensilla were only 2 long it would resonate in the 80-\~m region. Basiconica may measure from 2- to 8µm long so could resonate anywhere from 1.33 to 8µm depending on whether or not they represent a 1 λ (8µm) antenna or 6 λ (1.33µm antenna). In summary, frequencies involved in scent detection should lie in the near, middle or far i.r. (1 to 30µm) region as predicted for spines by Callahan (1964) and for pits by Grant (1949).”
